title: Gyri of the cerebral hemisphere (left lateral)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Location
Frontal lobe, directly in front of the central sulcus.
Function
Primary motor cortex: voluntary movement of the opposite side of the body. The body is mapped along it, with the leg at the top and medially and the face at the bottom.
hy: A lesion causes weakness of the opposite side of the body with upper motor neuron signs. The leg area lies in anterior cerebral artery territory and the arm and face areas in middle cerebral artery territory.

rows: Location
Parietal lobe, directly behind the central sulcus.
Function
Primary somatosensory cortex: touch, pain, temperature and position sense from the opposite side of the body, mapped in the same order as the motor cortex in front of it.
Location
Uppermost of the three horizontal gyri of the frontal lobe, above the superior frontal sulcus. It continues onto the medial surface of the hemisphere.
Function
Planning of movement (its medial part holds the supplementary motor area) and higher mental functions such as working memory.
Location
Frontal lobe, between the superior and inferior frontal sulci.
Function
Executive functions such as planning and working memory. Its posterior part holds the frontal eye field, which turns both eyes toward the opposite side.
hy: A lesion of the frontal eye field makes the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion.

rows: Location
Frontal lobe, below the inferior frontal sulcus and above the lateral sulcus.
Function
In the dominant hemisphere (usually the left) its posterior part is Broca area, which produces speech.
hy: A lesion of Broca area causes expressive aphasia: speech is slow and effortful but understanding is preserved, and the patient is aware of the problem.

rows: Location
Temporal lobe, between the lateral sulcus and the superior temporal sulcus.
Function
Hearing: the primary auditory cortex lies on its upper surface, inside the lateral sulcus. In the dominant hemisphere its posterior part is Wernicke area, which understands language.
hy: A lesion of Wernicke area causes receptive aphasia: speech is fluent but makes no sense, understanding is lost, and the patient is unaware of the problem.

rows: Location
Temporal lobe, between the superior and inferior temporal sulci.
Function
Processing of word meaning. The area for visual motion lies at its posterior end, where the temporal lobe meets the occipital lobe.
Location
Temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus. It continues onto the lower surface of the hemisphere.
Function
Recognition of objects by sight. Recognition of faces is centered on the neighboring fusiform gyrus, on the lower surface of the lobe.
Location
Inferior parietal lobule, curving around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus.
Function
Brings together touch, position sense and language. In the dominant hemisphere it takes part in the sound structure of words.
Location
Inferior parietal lobule, curving around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus.
Function
Brings together vision, hearing and touch for reading, writing and calculation.
hy: A lesion in the dominant hemisphere causes Gerstmann syndrome: inability to write, inability to calculate, inability to name the fingers, and confusion of left and right.

rows: Location
Posterior cranial fossa, behind the pons and medulla and below the tentorium cerebelli.
Function
Coordinates movement, balance and posture by comparing the movement that was intended with the movement that is taking place.
hy: Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion. A lesion of a hemisphere causes limb ataxia and intention tremor, with a tendency to fall toward that side; a lesion of the vermis causes a wide-based gait and unsteadiness of the trunk.
